---
title: Prepare observations
description: "Assemble one record per decision with the history known at that time and labels from the window after it."
engine: markdown
---

Suppose your source data contains a transaction table and a separate stream
of dispute reports. To support the review decision in the
[history tutorial](add-transaction-history.qmd), prepare a dataset with one
account review per row. relflow reads those observations; your application
decides which transactions belong to each review, what was known then, and
what the later labels mean. This page defines that data contract for the
payment examples.

## One row is one decision

The inputs to an observation describe what was known about one decision at
one moment. For this account review, they are the account's transactions
through the latest payment, in order. A historical training row also carries
the labels learned later: each `disputed` Boolean records whether a new
dispute against that transaction was reported in the 30 days after the
common review cutoff. None of those labels is an input.

The YAML below illustrates one such training row. Each transaction has its
booking time, amount, and merchant; the cutoff is immediately after the
final booking on May 28. `payment_id` identifies the review and
`transaction_id` identifies an item in its history:

```yaml
payment_id: payment-42
trxns:
  - transaction_id: trxn-40
    booked_at: "2026-05-21T10:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
    disputed: false
  - transaction_id: trxn-41
    booked_at: "2026-05-27T18:15:00"
    amount: 56.20
    merchant: North Market
    disputed: true
  - transaction_id: trxn-42
    booked_at: "2026-05-28T14:30:00"
    amount: 84.50
    merchant: North Market
    disputed: false
```

The latest payment is the final item of `trxns`. It needs no separate root
fields: the branch reads the booking time, amount, and merchant of every
transaction, including that one.

The outer row is the unit of batching and splitting. A batch of 128 rows
contains 128 account-review observations, with a transaction list inside each.
A branch's `length` limit controls those inner lists independently.

Keep `payment_id` at the root to identify the review and `transaction_id`
inside each item to identify that transaction. These identifiers remain
application metadata unless the model explicitly declares them as fields.

## Choose a decision time

Every observation has a cutoff, the moment the decision is made. Here it is
the account review immediately after the latest booking on May 28. The inputs
may contain only what was known then. Each label answers one question about
the following window: was a new dispute reported against this transaction in
the 30 days after the cutoff?

```{typst}
//| label: fig-decision-time
//| fig-cap: "Transactions booked before the review cutoff are inputs. Labels come from the 30 days after it. Events after the cutoff never enter the inputs."
//| fig-alt: "A timeline with three transactions on May 21, May 27, and May 28 before a dashed review cutoff at 14:30 on May 28. A shaded label window covers the next 30 days. An event on June 3 is excluded from the inputs, and a dispute reported inside the window defines a label."
#timeline(
  (
    (at: 3, label: [May 21]),
    (at: 9, label: [May 27], level: 1),
    (at: 10.6, label: [May 28, latest]),
    (at: 16, label: [June 3, excluded], kind: "excluded", level: 1),
    (at: 23, label: [Dispute reported], kind: "label"),
  ),
  cutoff: (at: 10.6, label: [Review cutoff: May 28, 14:30]),
  window: (from: 10.6, to: 40.6, label: [Label window: the next 30 days]),
  start: 0, end: 44,
)
```

Three consequences follow:

- **Every transaction is a target.** All three transactions are known at the
  cutoff, so each one gets a label for the same window, and the full sequence
  is valid context for each prediction. These are not forecasts made
  separately at each transaction's original booking time.
- **Labels arrive later.** Attach `disputed` only after the window has closed.
  A payment still waiting for its outcome is not a negative example.
- **Prediction records look the same without labels.** A request contains
  the same `trxns` records, cut at its own decision time, with `disputed`
  omitted.

## Order the history

Supply `trxns` oldest to newest. The model reads order from list position,
and `overflow="tail"` on a bounded branch keeps the most recent records,
including the latest payment, when a history is longer than its cap. relflow
does not sort, deduplicate, or join; do that before the row exists.

`booked_at` becomes recurring calendar positions through `DateParts`: day of
month, day of week, and hour of day. Those cycles say when something
happened, not how long ago. When the pace of activity matters, derive the gap
between transactions in a [preprocessor](../guides/preprocessing.qmd) and read
it as a `Number`.

## Split by time

Splits are separate collections of observations with different roles:

| Split | Purpose | Includes the settled target labels? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `train` | Update the model's learned parameters and data-dependent state. | Yes |
| `validate` | Choose model settings and the best checkpoint without training on these observations. | Yes |
| `test` | Assess the chosen model on observations held out from those choices. | Yes |
| `predict` | Score new decisions whose answers are not yet known. | No |

Train on earlier decision windows and validate on later ones. Build each
observation from information available at its own cutoff, and keep later
outcomes out of its inputs. The same account can appear at several decision
times; keep their label windows from overlapping the validation period.
relflow does not enforce these rules. [Evaluation](evaluation.qmd)
describes the comparisons that depend on them.

## Bind the record to the schema

The Parquet schema describes the stored values. Your model declaration also
chooses how each value is represented and which fields to predict; those
choices drive architecture generation.

With the record prepared, binding is a matter of names. The parent keyword
names each child, and each child reads the same-named value in its parent:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
    ),
)
```

`trxns` reads the list; its children read each transaction's fields. Columns
the schema does not name, such as `payment_id`, are ignored as inputs and can
be [retained in the output](read-predictions.qmd). A required
field missing from the Arrow schema is a binding error; an explicit null is a
value state governed by the field's `nullable` option.

When names or nesting differ from the schema, read them in place with a
[query](../guides/query-paths.qmd). When the source needs renaming, derived values,
filtering, joins, or reshaping, attach a
[preprocessor](../guides/preprocessing.qmd) to the data module. Its output is
what the model binds.

## Assemble histories from transaction tables

If your source has one row per transaction, prepare one review observation
before passing it to RelFlow:

1. Create the review decisions with an account identifier, `payment_id`, and
   cutoff time. The payment being reviewed is the latest item at that cutoff.
2. Join each decision to that account's transactions. Keep only transactions
   booked by the cutoff and known to the application then. Deduplicate by
   transaction identifier, sort oldest to newest, and use a stable tie-breaker
   for equal booking times. The latest payment appears exactly once.
3. For a labeled observation, attach each transaction's `disputed` answer
   from reports in the 30 days after that review's cutoff. Wait for the whole
   window to finish before labeling the absence of a report as `false`.
4. Group by review decision, collecting the ordered transaction fields into
   the `trxns` list. Keep the review's `payment_id` outside it and each
   `transaction_id` inside its item. Assign whole review observations to their
   time-based splits, then export them.

One account can contribute several observations, each with its own cutoff and
labels. Grouping by account alone would collapse those decisions together
and could introduce future transactions into earlier observations. Your
application's SQL, Arrow, or Polars preparation must preserve the decision
boundary.

## Supply the files used by the tutorials

Export each collection of prepared observations as Parquet, preserving `trxns`
as a list of records with typed fields. The history tutorial uses:

| Example path | Row contents |
| --- | --- |
| `payments/history/train.parquet` | Historical review observations with every transaction's settled `disputed` label. |
| `payments/history/validation.parquet` | Separate, later review observations with the same structure and labels. |
| `payments/history/requests.parquet` | New review observations with `disputed` omitted from each transaction. |

These paths name files your application creates. `ArrowDataModule` reads the
files you pass to it; assigning a split does not assemble histories or divide
one file into train and validation rows. The flat tutorial uses separate
`payments/flat/` files because each of its rows is a single payment.

Keep both kinds of identifier in request files so
[Read predictions](read-predictions.qmd) can associate every answer with its
source transaction. [Preprocessing](../guides/preprocessing.qmd) shows
additional transforms on prepared records. For existing Arrow or Polars
tables, databases, and streamed sources, see [Data modules](../guides/data-modules.qmd).

Next, [train and save](train-and-save.qmd) the model on files
prepared this way.
